# 4.6 – Graphing Linear Inequalities {.unnumbered}

You’ve learned how to **graph lines** from equations like $y = 2x + 3$.
Now we’ll take that same idea and add one new twist — an **inequality symbol**.

When we switch from **equations** to **inequalities**, we’re no longer looking for one line that fits. We’re looking for **all the points that make the inequality true** — a whole region of the graph.

:::{.objectives}

* [ ] I can graph linear inequalities in two variables.
* [ ] I can explain what the shaded region means in a real-world context.

:::

:::{.vocab}

{{< glink inequality >}}, {{< glink greater than >}}, {{< glink less than >}}, {{< glink dashed line >}}, {{< glink solid line >}}, {{< glink solution set >}}

:::

{{< warmup >}}

1. Solve for $x$: $4x - 7 < 13$
2. Solve for $y$: $-3y + 6 \ge 9$
3. On a graph, what does it mean if a point is *above* the line $y = 2x + 3$? What about *below* it?

{{< learn >}}

### 4.6.1 – Linear Inequalities in Two Variables

When we graph an inequality like
$$y < 2x + 3,$$
we start just like a line — by graphing the **boundary** $y = 2x + 3$.

But the inequality sign changes what happens next:

* If it’s **<** or **>**, we draw a **dashed line**.

  > (Points *on* the line are *not* included.)
* If it’s **≤** or **≥**, we draw a **solid line**.

  > (Points *on* the line *are* included.)

Then we **shade** the half of the graph where the inequality is true:

* Shade **above** the line for **greater than** ($>$ or $≥$).
* Shade **below** the line for **less than** ($<$ or $≤$).

:::{.you-try-m title="Graph and shade"}
Graph $y > -x + 2$.
Is the line solid or dashed? Which side should you shade?
:::

---

### 4.6.2 – Systems of Inequalities

A **system of inequalities** means you have *more than one* inequality on the same graph.
Each one creates a shaded region, and the **solution set** is where the shaded regions **overlap**.

This area represents all points that make **every inequality true at once**.

:::{.real-world title="Example – Budget and Time Limits"}
You can make bracelets ($x$) and necklaces ($y$).
Each bracelet takes 1 hour, each necklace takes 2 hours, and you have at most 10 hours total.
You also can’t make negative amounts.

Inequalities:
$$
\begin{aligned}
x + 2y &\le 10 \\
x &\ge 0 \\
y &\ge 0
\end{aligned}
$$
Graph these and shade the region that satisfies all three.
:::

---

### 4.6.3 – Interpreting the Shaded Region

Every point in the shaded area represents a **possible solution**.
In real-world terms, that might mean:

* combinations of products you can afford,
* time or resource limits you can’t exceed,
* or any mix of values that meet your conditions.

:::{.you-try-m title="Practice Interpretation"}
You’re buying snacks for a party. Chips cost $3 per bag and drinks cost $2 each.
You can spend at most $12.

1. Write an inequality for your total cost.
2. Graph it.
3. What does a point inside the shaded region mean?
:::
